Here we show how to check that inference returns the posterior it should, on average over the prior.
This is simulation-based calibration [@talts_validating_2020; @modrak_simulation_2025].
Each replicate draws parameter values from the prior, simulates a study at them, fits it back with the same model, and ranks each drawn value among the posterior draws of its fit.
When the likelihood and the sampler are correct, the drawn value behaves as one more posterior draw, so its rank is uniform over the replicates.

[Parameter recovery checks](parameter_recovery_checks.html) hold the truth at one value and measure how far the estimates land from it.
Calibration draws a new truth for every replicate and checks the posterior as a whole: its 50% intervals contain the truth in half of the replicates, its 90% intervals in nine out of ten, and so on for every level.

We use the same final-size example presented in [Get started](housepi.html):

```{r}
#| label: model-setup
# define the model as in 'Get Started'
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)
set.seed(42)

hh_model <- flu_1918_frederick |>
  new_housepi_model("final-size") |>
  add_parameter(import = "template")

get_parameters(hh_model)
```

The check needs no fit to the Frederick data.
The truth of each replicate is drawn from the uniform priors of `alpha`, `beta` and `gamma`, while `hh_size_ref` is held constant at 4.
The data only lends its households to the simulated studies.

# Rank the prior draws

`check_calibration()` simulates each study on households drawn with replacement from the attached data by `sample_house_structure()`, as many as in Frederick.
Each fit runs the default MCMC configuration of `run_inference()`, here on two threads.
The drawn value is ranked among 99 draws thinned evenly from these 800, so its rank takes one of `rank_levels = 100` values, 0 to 99:

```{r}
#| label: calibration
calibration <- hh_model |>
  check_calibration(nrep = 100, threads = 2)
calibration

# overview of the sweep, averaged over replicates
calibration$overview
```

A rank is uniform only if the 99 draws it is taken among behave like independent ones.
A parameter is flagged when its bulk effective sample size [@vehtari_rank_normalization_2021] falls below 99,
or when its fit fails the convergence diagnostics: here `r calibration$overview$n_flagged` of `r calibration$nrep` replicates were flagged.

The rank of every parameter in every replicate is stored in `calibration$estimates`.
Uniform ranks fill each bin of ten ranks with about `r calibration$nrep / 10` replicates:

```{r}
#| label: rank-histogram
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Three histograms, one per parameter, of the ranks of the drawn values
#|  among 99 posterior draws, in bins of ten ranks, against a horizontal
#|  line at the count expected for uniform ranks.
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(calibration$estimates, aes(x = rank)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 0, closed = "left") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = calibration$nrep / 10, colour = "coral") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable) +
  labs(x = "rank", y = "replicates")
```

Ranks piling at both ends mean the posterior is too narrow, so the truth falls in its tails too often.
Ranks piling in the middle mean it is too wide.
Ranks piling on one side mean it is shifted: low ranks put the truth below most posterior draws, so the model overestimates the parameter.

# Test for uniformity

```{r}
#| label: bin-counts
#| include: false
bins <- table(calibration$estimates$variable, calibration$estimates$rank %/% 10)
```

With 100 replicates a bin of ten ranks holds 10 on average, give or take 3, and the picture changes with the bin width.
Here the bins hold from `r min(bins)` to `r max(bins)` ranks.
@sailynoja_graphical_2022 compare instead the empirical CDF of the ranks with the uniform CDF, inside a band that a uniform ECDF stays within at every point at once with 95% probability.
bayesplot draws this band with `ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped()`, from the ranks rescaled to $[0, 1]$:

```{r}
#| label: rank-ecdf
#| fig-height: 3
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Three panels, one per parameter. Each shows the difference between the
#|  empirical CDF of the scaled ranks and the uniform CDF, as a solid step
#|  line, inside a dashed band around zero.
rank_levels <- calibration$rank_levels

bayesplot::ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped(
  pit = calibration$estimates$rank / (rank_levels - 1),
  group = calibration$estimates$variable,
  K = rank_levels, prob = 0.95, plot_diff = TRUE
) +
  labs(x = "scaled rank")
```

A posterior that overestimates puts the curve above zero, since low ranks make the ECDF rise early, and one that underestimates puts it below.
A posterior too narrow draws an S, above zero on the left and below on the right; one too wide draws the mirror image.

`calibration$summarise()` reads the same test: `uniform` is `FALSE` when the ECDF leaves the band at any point, which happens to uniform ranks in at most 5% of checks.

```{r}
#| label: summary
calibration$summarise()
```

```{r}
#| label: verdict
#| include: false
verdict <- calibration$summarise()
n_uniform <- sum(verdict$uniform)
```

Here `r n_uniform` of `r nrow(verdict)` parameters pass.
Passing says that the sampler and the likelihood agree with the prior and the model.
It says nothing about whether the model fits Frederick: for that, compare its predictions with the data in [Predictive checks](predictive_checks.html).

# A sampler run too short

Calibration also catches a sampler run too short for its draws to stand for the posterior.
We repeat the check with two chains of 50 steps, the first 25 of each spent adapting the proposals, and keep every draw:

```{r}
#| label: short-chains
short <- hh_model |>
  check_calibration(nrep = 100, steps = 50, thin = 1, adapt = 25,
                    chains = 2, threads = 2)
short_summary <- short$summarise()
short_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: short-chains-ecdf
#| fig-height: 3
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Same three panels as above, for the ranks of the short chains.
bayesplot::ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped(
  pit = short$estimates$rank / (rank_levels - 1),
  group = short$estimates$variable,
  K = rank_levels, prob = 0.95, plot_diff = TRUE
) +
  labs(x = "scaled rank")
```

```{r}
#| label: short-verdict
#| include: false
code_words <- \(x) knitr::combine_words(x, before = "`")
failed <- short_summary$variable[!short_summary$uniform]
passed <- short_summary$variable[short_summary$uniform]
extreme <- with(short$estimates,
                tapply(rank %in% c(0, rank_levels - 1), variable, mean))
```

`r sum(short$replicates$flagged)` of `r short$nrep` replicates are flagged, since 100 correlated draws are worth far fewer than 99 independent ones.
Correlated draws sit closer together than the posterior they come from, so the truth falls outside all of them too often.
Rank 0 or 99 takes `r knitr::combine_words(paste0(round(100 * extreme), "% of the ranks of \x60", names(extreme), "\x60"))`, against 2% for uniform ranks.
The ranks of `r code_words(failed)` fail the test: their ECDF jumps at both ends and draws the S of a posterior too narrow, an excess that the first and last bins of a histogram would dilute among ten ranks each.
`r if (length(passed)) paste("The ranks of", code_words(passed), "pass on flagged fits, which is no evidence of calibration.")`

# Calibrate on the data

The checks above average over the prior.
Most truths drawn from the uniform priors of `alpha`, `beta` and `gamma` lie far from the values the Frederick data supports.
Inference can be calibrated on average over the prior and still fail where the posterior of Frederick puts its mass, or fail somewhere the data rules out [@sailynoja_posterior_2026].

Posterior calibration conditions the check on the data.
Each replicate takes one posterior draw of the Frederick fit as its truth, simulates a study at it, and fits that study together with the Frederick households.
The truth is then one more draw of the posterior given both, so its rank among the draws of that fit is uniform when inference is correct.
Passing `draws` to `check_calibration()` runs it:

```{r}
#| label: posterior-calibration
hh_fit <- run_inference(hh_model, threads = 2)
posterior_calibration <- hh_model |>
  check_calibration(hh_fit, nrep = 100, threads = 2)
posterior_calibration
```

The truths are 100 distinct posterior draws, picked evenly among the draws of the fit thinned to their effective sample size, so the fit must hold at least 100 independent draws.
Each replicate fits twice the Frederick households, the observed ones and as many simulated, so it costs more than a replicate of the prior check.
The ranks read with the same test:

```{r}
#| label: posterior-ecdf
#| fig-height: 3
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Same three panels as above, for the ranks of the posterior draws.
bayesplot::ppc_pit_ecdf_grouped(
  pit = posterior_calibration$estimates$rank / (rank_levels - 1),
  group = posterior_calibration$estimates$variable,
  K = rank_levels, prob = 0.95, plot_diff = TRUE
) +
  labs(x = "scaled rank")

posterior_calibration$summarise()
```

```{r}
#| label: posterior-verdict
#| include: false
posterior_verdict <- posterior_calibration$summarise()
```

Here `r sum(posterior_verdict$uniform)` of `r nrow(posterior_verdict)` parameters pass.
The draws must come from `run_inference()` on this model and data: draws fitted to other data, or a table of values, are refused.
Prior calibration tells whether inference works for any study the model could describe.
Posterior calibration tells whether it works for Frederick.
